screens.title: Operational Management with AWS Systems Manager (SSM)
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn how AWS Systems Manager gives you a single operational control plane for EC2 instances and on-premises servers. We'll ground the ideas in concrete tasks: securely accessing an instance without opening SSH, running commands across many servers, automating OS patching, storing secrets safely, and orchestrating repeatable workflows. For an architect, these capabilities reduce operational complexity by removing ad-hoc SSH access, enabling large-scale scripted actions, and making routine maintenance auditable and repeatable. For example, using Session Manager you can open a shell session through the AWS control plane and have all activity logged in CloudWatch or S3. Run Command makes applying the same change to dozens or hundreds of instances reliable and trackable. Parameter Store replaces hardcoded credentials with encrypted parameters that your application reads at runtime. Throughout this chapter you will see concrete steps, permissions to watch for, common mistakes such as overbroad IAM policies, and patterns for testing changes in non-production first. By the end you should be able to design operational workflows that are secure, automated, and auditable. Consider which of your current maintenance tasks could run under SSM instead of manual SSH sessions.

screens.title: What is AWS Systems Manager (SSM)?
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Systems Manager is a collection of capabilities that provide a unified operational interface for managing AWS resources and on-premises servers. At its core, SSM offers a control plane for operations: an agent runs on each managed host, services like Session Manager and Run Command perform access and actions, and supporting features handle patching, configuration, and orchestration. The defining claim is that SSM reduces manual, error-prone work by making operations programmatic, auditable, and repeatable. For example, instead of logging into an instance by SSH to update a configuration file on dozens of servers, you can store the value in Parameter Store and roll out a Run Command or Automation document to update every instance. A common misconception is that SSM only applies to EC2; in reality, the SSM Agent can run on on-premises servers as well, enabling hybrid operational control. Another misconception is that SSM replaces configuration management tools entirely — it complements them by providing targeted run-time actions, secure parameter storage, and native AWS orchestration. Takeaway: think of SSM as your operational toolbox for secure, large-scale, and auditable management of compute resources.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.3 › What is SSM?
Definition

A suite of capabilities that automate operational tasks across EC2 instances and on-premises servers through an agent and control-plane services.

Why it matters
It reduces manual SSH, enables fleet-wide changes, and provides audit trails for compliance.
Concrete example
Store a DB password in Parameter Store and update applications to retrieve it at runtime rather than hardcoding credentials.
Key Takeaway

SSM centralizes automation and access, improving security and repeatability for operational tasks.

Analogy
Think of SSM as a remote operations console that sits between you and servers, letting you push actions and retrieve logs without direct network access into instances.
Common misconceptions
  • SSM only works for EC2 — false; the SSM Agent can register on-premises servers as managed instances.
  • SSM replaces all config management — false; it complements tools by adding AWS-native operational actions and secrets management.
Check your understanding
Name one operational task you currently do by SSH that could be automated with SSM and why automation improves it.

screens.title: SSM Agent and instance registration
screens.narratorSegment: The SSM Agent is the component installed on EC2 or on-premises hosts that enables Systems Manager to manage those instances. The agent establishes outbound connections to AWS SSM endpoints so the service can orchestrate actions and forward session data. To use SSM you must ensure the SSM Agent is installed and running and that the instance has an IAM instance profile with the required permissions such as AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore. A concrete example: when you launch an Amazon Linux 2 instance with the proper instance profile, the preinstalled agent registers itself and becomes visible as a managed instance in Systems Manager. A common mistake is forgetting the instance profile or opening this up to a role that lacks kms:Decrypt when using encrypted parameters — the agent may register but cannot retrieve encrypted data. Another misconception is that agent installation alone is sufficient; the network path to SSM endpoints must be available, and the instance profile must grant permission. Takeaway: verify agent, network reachability, and instance profile permissions together before relying on SSM in production. How would you validate these three components in your environment?

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.3 › Agent & Registration
Registration steps
  1. Install and run the SSM Agent on the host.
  2. Attach an IAM instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore.
  3. Ensure outbound network access to SSM endpoints.
  4. Confirm the instance appears as a managed instance in Systems Manager.
Common mistake

Assuming the agent alone is enough. Without correct IAM permissions and network access the instance will not be fully manageable.

Example: Amazon Linux 2
Launch an instance with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore attached. The preinstalled agent registers automatically in a few minutes; confirm in the Systems Manager console or via the AWS CLI that the managed instance appears.
Check 1: Agent
Verify the agent service is running on the instance.
Check 2: IAM Role
Confirm the instance profile includes SSM permissions and KMS decrypt if needed.
Why this matters
Reliable registration is the foundation for Session Manager, Run Command, Patch Manager, and Automation. If registration breaks, none of these features can act on the host.

screens.title: Session Manager: secure, auditable access
screens.narratorSegment: Session Manager provides secure, auditable shell or PowerShell access to instances without opening inbound SSH or RDP ports. The core idea is that the SSM Agent on the instance initiates an outbound connection to the Systems Manager service, and the console or AWS CLI uses that control plane to broker an interactive session. All session activity can be logged to CloudWatch Logs or S3, creating a full audit trail of who connected and which commands ran. For example, instead of creating a bastion host and opening port 22, you launch instances with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore role and use Session Manager to get a shell. A common misconception is that Session Manager removes the need for all network controls; it reduces the need for inbound ports, but you still must manage outbound network egress and IAM permissions. Also, make sure session logging is enabled to meet compliance needs. Takeaway: Session Manager reduces the attack surface and improves auditing, but it must be configured with correct IAM policies and logging destinations. Consider asking: how will your audit process ingest session logs for investigations?

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.3 › Session Manager
How it works
  • SSM Agent opens outbound connection to Systems Manager.
  • Console or CLI requests a session; the control plane brokers an interactive shell.
  • Session activity can be logged to CloudWatch Logs or S3 for audit trails.
Concrete example
Start a Session Manager session in the console and run a diagnostic command; the entire session is recorded if logging is enabled.
Key Takeaway

Session Manager removes the need for inbound SSH/RDP, lowering exposure while enabling full session logs for compliance.

Permissions & logging to check
IAM instance profile
Include AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore so the agent can communicate with SSM.
Session logging
Enable CloudWatch or S3 logging to capture commands and outputs for audit.
Common pitfall
Failing to enable logging will remove the audit trail, undermining the compliance benefit of Session Manager.

screens.title: SSM Run Command: execute across a fleet
screens.narratorSegment: Run Command lets you execute scripts or predefined SSM documents across one or thousands of managed instances. You choose targets by instance IDs, tags, or resource groups and select documents like AWS-RunShellScript. The service runs the command concurrently and returns per-instance status and output, which can be written to CloudWatch Logs or S3 for later inspection. An example workflow: use Run Command with AWS-RunShellScript to place a file on all web servers, then review execution results to ensure success. A frequent operational error is granting overly broad Run Command permissions; users should only be allowed to run approved documents or target specific resource groups. Another pitfall is not handling partial failures — always inspect per-instance output for failures and design retries or notifications into your automation. Takeaway: Run Command is a powerful fleet orchestration tool, but it requires careful IAM scoping and attention to result aggregation for reliable operations. What retry or notification approach would you add to your Run Command workflows? SSM Run Command: execute across a fleet means run command executes scripts across targets, reports per-instance results, and integrates with cloudwatch or s3 for output and auditing.. In practical terms, targeting, documents, and collecting output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.3 › Run Command
Key steps
  1. Choose a document (for example AWS-RunShellScript).
  2. Specify command parameters.
  3. Target instances by tag, ID, or resource group.
  4. Run and monitor per-instance status and output.
Example
Run a command to write a file: echo "Hello from Run Command!" > /tmp/runcommand_test.txt and later verify via a session or output files.
Key Takeaway

Run Command enables reliable, auditable execution across many instances, but design for partial failures and least-privilege access.

Permissions & outputs
Targeting
Use tags or resource groups so deployments remain organized and limited to intended hosts.
Output
Collect per-instance command output to S3 or CloudWatch for later analysis and auditing.
Common pitfall
Allowing broad user permissions to run arbitrary documents, which can lead to unexpected changes across many servers.

screens.title: Run Command vs Session Manager
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between Run Command and Session Manager depends on the task you need to perform. Run Command is ideal for non-interactive, repeatable tasks across multiple instances: install packages, change configuration files, create files, or gather diagnostics in parallel. Session Manager is for interactive troubleshooting or when you need a shell to investigate state in real time. A concrete example: to deploy a configuration file to 50 servers, Run Command with AWS-RunShellScript is efficient and auditable. If a single instance exhibits strange behavior and you need to explore logs interactively, use Session Manager. A common misconception is thinking Session Manager is always safer; both are secure when used properly, but Run Command minimizes human error at scale and supports output collection automatically. Another misconception is believing Run Command can't be audited — it provides per-instance results and can send output to CloudWatch or S3. Takeaway: use Run Command for scripted, fleet-wide actions and Session Manager for interactive troubleshooting; combine them in Automation documents when a workflow needs both. In practical terms, when to use interactive sessions and when to run commands. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 07 › Chapter 7.3 › Run Command vs Session Manager
Run Command
  • Non-interactive, parallel execution across targets.
  • Ideal for installs, config changes, and diagnostics at scale.
  • Collects per-instance output for auditing.
Example
Deploy a config file across 50 nodes and confirm success through collected outputs.
Session Manager
  • Interactive shell or PowerShell access without opening inbound ports.
  • Best for troubleshooting where you need to run commands and inspect state in real time.
  • Session logs are auditable if logging is enabled.
Example
Investigate a single server's logs and run interactive diagnostics, then close the session with a logged trail.

screens.title: SSM Patch Manager
screens.narratorSegment: Patch Manager automates scanning and applying patches to managed instances based on patch baselines you define. A patch baseline specifies which patches are approved, rejected, or require manual approval. You target instances and define patch windows that control when updates run to avoid impacting business hours. For example, you can create a baseline that approves only security updates and schedule a weekly maintenance window for non-production and a different window for production. Patch Manager supports pre- and post-patching actions so you can run tests or backups before applying updates. A common mistake is applying untested baselines directly to production; always stage baselines in non-production environments to validate compatibility. Also, ensure automation includes monitoring for failures and a rollback or remediation plan. Takeaway: Patch Manager keeps instances up-to-date reliably, but treat baselines and schedules as part of your release discipline to avoid service disruption. SSM Patch Manager means patch manager enforces patch baselines and schedules to scan and apply approved updates while allowing pre- and post-actions for verification.. In practical terms, automating os patching and update windows. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.3 › Patch Manager
Patch baseline essentials
  • Define which patches are approved, rejected, or require review.
  • Schedule patch windows to control when updates run.
  • Use pre- and post-patching actions for backups and tests.
Key Takeaway

Use Patch Manager to automate security updates with controlled windows and test baselines before production deployment.

Example schedule
Set a weekly non-production patch window for testing and a monthly production window that includes verification steps. Use the scan results to review missing patches before applying them.
Common pitfall
Applying untested baselines to production can cause unexpected failures; always validate in staging.

screens.title: SSM Parameter Store
screens.narratorSegment: Parameter Store provides a hierarchical key-value store for configuration data and secrets. Parameters can be plain text or SecureString, which uses AWS KMS to encrypt and decrypt values. This enables you to keep database passwords, A P I keys, or license codes out of instance files and source code. A common workflow is to store a SecureString for a database password, grant the instance role ssm:GetParameter and kms:Decrypt permissions, and have the application fetch the parameter at startup. A mistake to avoid is granting wide kms:Decrypt permissions — scope decryption to the specific KMS key used for the parameter. Another misconception is that Parameter Store is a secret management replacement for every use case; for advanced rotation workflows you may still need a secrets manager, but Parameter Store is sufficient for many encrypted configuration scenarios. Takeaway: Parameter Store centralizes configuration and secrets with KMS encryption support; make sure IAM roles and key policies are narrowly scoped so retrieval works only for authorized principals. Module 07 › Chapter 7.3 › Lab Walkthrough
Terminal demo steps
Follow these steps in your console and terminal to validate SSM end-to-end. The commands here illustrate intent; run them where your role and instance context apply.
# Launch instance with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore attached (console)
# Wait for instance to register

# Start a Session Manager session (console or CLI):
aws ssm start-session --target i-0123456789abcdef0

# Run Command example (AWS-RunShellScript):
# Command: echo "Hello from Run Command!" > /tmp/runcommand_test.txt

# Create a SecureString parameter (console or CLI):

screens.title: Security and operational best practices
screens.narratorSegment: When designing SSM workflows, several best practices reduce risk and increase reliability. First, apply least-privilege access: do not grant wide Run Command or Parameter Store permissions. Scope ssm:GetParameter and kms:Decrypt to specific parameter and key ARNs. Second, test automation documents and patch baselines in non-production to identify compatibility issues before rolling out to production. Third, enable session and Run Command logging to CloudWatch or S3 to maintain an audit trail for investigations and compliance. Fourth, use tags and resource groups to target actions precisely and avoid accidental cross-environment changes. A common operational mistake is running fleet-wide commands without partial-failure handling. Always design a process to review per-instance results and to retry or roll back when necessary. Another misconception is thinking logging alone solves all compliance needs; logs should be integrated into retention and monitoring pipelines for alerts and analysis. Takeaway: combine strict IAM scoping, staged testing, and comprehensive logging to ensure SSM automations are safe to operate at scale. In this chapter you'll learn how AWS Systems Manager gives you a single operational control plane for EC2 instances and on-premises servers. We'll ground the ideas in concrete tasks: securely accessing an instance without opening SSH, running commands across many servers, automating OS patching, storing secrets safely, and orchestrating repeatable workflows. For an architect, these capabilities reduce operational complexity by removing ad-hoc SSH access, enabling large-scale scripted actions, and making routine maintenance auditable and repeatable. For example, using Session Manager you can open a shell session through the AWS control plane and have all activity logged in CloudWatch or S3. Run Command makes applying the same change to dozens or hundreds of instances reliable and trackable. Parameter Store replaces hardcoded credentials with encrypted parameters that your application reads at runtime. Throughout this chapter you will see concrete steps, permissions to watch for, common mistakes such as overbroad IAM policies, and patterns for testing changes in non-production first. By the end you should be able to design operational workflows that are secure, automated, and auditable. Consider which of your current maintenance tasks could run under SSM instead of manual SSH sessions.

By the end of this chapter you will identify core SSM capabilities and use them to secure and automate instance management. You should be able to explain how Session Manager provides auditable browser-based access without opening SSH, and why that reduces the attack surface. You'll learn to run commands across hundreds of instances using Run Command, target by tags or instance IDs, and collect execution output for auditing. You will also understand Patch Manager for automated OS updates, how to define patch baselines, and why you should test baselines in non-production first. Parameter Store will become your tool for secure, hierarchical configuration storage and secrets management with KMS encryption. Finally, you will be able to design Automation documents to orchestrate complex workflows like creating AMIs or remediating non-compliant resources, and recognize when to use Automation versus chaining Run Commands. Each objective maps to a verified competency milestone so you can measure practical mastery.

These objectives emphasize hands-on capability. You'll be able to start a session without opening port 22, run a command across multiple instances, create and retrieve a secure parameter, design a patch baseline, and author a simple Automation document to perform a sequence of steps. For example, the hands-on lab walks you through launching an EC2 instance with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore role, avoiding SSH in the security group, then using Session Manager to run a shell command and Run Command to create a file across targets. You will also practice storing a SecureString in Parameter Store and retrieving it from an instance using the AWS CLI, which requires ssm:GetParameter and kms:Decrypt permissions for the instance role. These are operational skills you can use immediately: they reduce manual effort, make actions auditable, and help maintain compliance. Remember to test in a staging environment and avoid overly broad IAM permissions for Run Command or Parameter Store access.

AWS Systems Manager is a collection of capabilities that provide a unified operational interface for managing AWS resources and on-premises servers. At its core, SSM offers a control plane for operations: an agent runs on each managed host, services like Session Manager and Run Command perform access and actions, and supporting features handle patching, configuration, and orchestration. The defining claim is that SSM reduces manual, error-prone work by making operations programmatic, auditable, and repeatable. For example, instead of logging into an instance by SSH to update a configuration file on dozens of servers, you can store the value in Parameter Store and roll out a Run Command or Automation document to update every instance. A common misconception is that SSM only applies to EC2; in reality, the SSM Agent can run on on-premises servers as well, enabling hybrid operational control. Another misconception is that SSM replaces configuration management tools entirely — it complements them by providing targeted run-time actions, secure parameter storage, and native AWS orchestration. Takeaway: think of SSM as your operational toolbox for secure, large-scale, and auditable management of compute resources.

The SSM Agent is the component installed on EC2 or on-premises hosts that enables Systems Manager to manage those instances. The agent establishes outbound connections to AWS SSM endpoints so the service can orchestrate actions and forward session data. To use SSM you must ensure the SSM Agent is installed and running and that the instance has an IAM instance profile with the required permissions such as AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore. A concrete example: when you launch an Amazon Linux 2 instance with the proper instance profile, the preinstalled agent registers itself and becomes visible as a managed instance in Systems Manager. A common mistake is forgetting the instance profile or opening this up to a role that lacks kms:Decrypt when using encrypted parameters — the agent may register but cannot retrieve encrypted data. Another misconception is that agent installation alone is sufficient; the network path to SSM endpoints must be available, and the instance profile must grant permission. Takeaway: verify agent, network reachability, and instance profile permissions together before relying on SSM in production. How would you validate these three components in your environment?

Session Manager provides secure, auditable shell or PowerShell access to instances without opening inbound SSH or RDP ports. The core idea is that the SSM Agent on the instance initiates an outbound connection to the Systems Manager service, and the console or AWS CLI uses that control plane to broker an interactive session. All session activity can be logged to CloudWatch Logs or S3, creating a full audit trail of who connected and which commands ran. For example, instead of creating a bastion host and opening port 22, you launch instances with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore role and use Session Manager to get a shell. A common misconception is that Session Manager removes the need for all network controls; it reduces the need for inbound ports, but you still must manage outbound network egress and IAM permissions. Also, make sure session logging is enabled to meet compliance needs. Takeaway: Session Manager reduces the attack surface and improves auditing, but it must be configured with correct IAM policies and logging destinations. Consider asking: how will your audit process ingest session logs for investigations?

Run Command lets you execute scripts or predefined SSM documents across one or thousands of managed instances.
